text: The majority said this posted notice failed. The dissent answered with an image: unattended mailboxes, it wrote, are subject to plunder by thieves.
provenance: The dissent offered the counter-image that has outlived everything else in it.

text: That argument belonged to the dissent. A mailed letter can be stolen or misdelivered, while posting at least reaches the tenant's door.
The dissent said the majority preferred the Postal Service without proving that mail worked better than a notice fixed to the home.
provenance: The majority never proved the mails were better.

text: It also attacked the evidence: scant and conflicting testimony from only a handful of Kentucky process servers.
The dissent counted at least eleven States that allowed notice solely by posting or by leaving it at the residence.
provenance: It listed them in a footnote. At least eleven.

text: The majority's answer was narrower: whatever posting does elsewhere, on this record it did not reliably provide actual notice.
provenance: The majority never proved the mails were better. It proved this door was worse.

text: No vote tally is printed in the opinion, so this is not a story about a guessed five-to-four or six-to-three split.
provenance: The majority's opinion does not answer that one.

text: It is a dispute about imperfect delivery systems, ending where the dissent began: with a letter sitting in an unattended mailbox.
